interactions.summary: A student identifies David as the man after God's own heart, and Jiang intensifies the answer by saying David is the person God loves most in the Bible.
A student reads Dante's scriptural grounding for hope, where hope is marked by promises from scripture, Isaiah's double garment, and the answering cry of the heavenly circle.
Jiang glosses Isaiah as a persecuted prophet and compresses the citation into the broader rule that prophets are persecuted.
The next read passage introduces another radiant soul associated with Christ and a great task, while Beatrice watches the scene with bridal intensity.

Jiang interprets Beatrice's gloss as yet another intervention on Dante's behalf, now comparing Dante not only to Moses and David but even to Jesus, and again calls that the arrogance that produces greatness.

claims.claim: Jiang endorses the student's identification of David as the man after God's own heart and heightens it into the claim that David is the person God loves most.
The read passage grounds hope in scripture itself, with Dante saying both new and ancient scripture set the mark of what hope promises to souls befriended by God.

claims.claim: The Isaiah citation is treated as promising the elect a 'double garment' in blessed life, linking hope to an embodied reward rather than a purely abstract consolation.

claims.claim: Jiang summarizes Isaiah as a persecuted prophet and generalizes the point into a rule that prophets are persecuted.
Jiang reads Beatrice's explanation of Dante's mission as comparing Dante to Jesus, not just to Moses and David, because Dante is described as chosen for a great salvific task.
He insists that this inflation of Dante's rank is not an accidental excess but the very arrogance that drives Dante to literary greatness.

signature_moments.moment: Hope is not left as a mood; Dante treats scripture as a set of marks and promises that can be cited all the way down to the elect's 'double garment.'
signature_moments.source_phrase: the new and ancient scripture set the mark
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows Jiang's Dante grounding spiritual confidence in a scriptural architecture rather than in sentiment alone.

signature_moments.moment: Beatrice keeps escalating Dante's analogies upward until Jiang can say the poem is bold enough to compare him with Jesus himself.
signature_moments.source_phrase: he's also being compared to jesus
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This keeps the lecture's central pressure in view: Dante's sanctity is being built through outrageous poetic self-placement, not modest self-erasure.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: A scriptural image cited here as part of what hope promises to the elect in blessed life, later tied more concretely to embodied heavenly status.
Dante's way of naming the people marked by scriptural promise and therefore eligible for hope's fulfillment.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's quick gloss on Isaiah compresses several scriptural issues into a persecution theme; preserve it as Jiang's lecture framing rather than as a precise paraphrase of Isaiah's text.
